questions.question: Explain what electroplating is, give three examples of plated objects, and state the three reasons for plating.
questions.expected_answer: Electroplating is coating one metal with a thin layer of another by passing a direct current through a solution containing ions of the coating metal, so that the metal is deposited on the object; the layer is thousandths of a millimetre thick but hard, smooth and bright because it is metal bonded to metal. Examples: chromium plating on taps, bumpers and motorcycle parts; nickel plating on coins, cutlery and tools; gold plating on jewellery and electrical connectors; zinc plating on bolts and screws; tin plating inside food cans. Reasons: preservation, since the coat seals the base metal from oxygen and water and zinc also protects sacrificially; appearance, giving cheap steel the look of chrome, gold or silver; and properties, such as a hard wear-resistant chrome surface, a food-safe tin surface or a non-oxidising gold contact.

questions.question: Name the four parts of an electroplating cell and explain how metal is transferred from the anode to the object being plated.
questions.expected_answer: The electrolyte is a solution of a salt of the coating metal, such as copper sulphate, in which the metal exists as positive ions. The anode is a piece of the coating metal connected to the positive terminal. The cathode is the object to be plated, connected to the negative terminal. The supply is a low-voltage direct current source such as a battery. When current flows, positive metal ions are attracted to the negative object, take electrons there and become metal atoms, building a layer on its surface; at the positive anode, metal atoms give up electrons and dissolve into the solution as new ions, so the anode shrinks, the object gains a coat and the solution's strength is maintained. The mass deposited depends on the current and the time, so plating is controlled by an ammeter and a timer, with a low steady current giving a bright even coat.

questions.question: Describe the investigation of copper plating a steel key, including safety, method, recording and the reversed-leads test.
questions.expected_answer: Safety: copper sulphate is harmful if swallowed and irritates skin and eyes, so gloves and safety glasses are worn, hands are washed afterwards and the solution is kept for reuse. Method: sand the key bright all over, wash it in detergent, rinse and handle it only by its clip; half fill a jar with copper sulphate solution; clip a copper strip to the positive lead of a 3 to 4.5 volt battery and hang it in the solution; clip the key to the negative lead and hang it facing the copper without touching; connect and time. A pink film appears within a minute or two and a visible copper coat after ten minutes; the key is rinsed, dried and examined. Recording: time, voltage, whether the coat is bright and even or dark and powdery, and any bare patches and their cause such as a fingerprint. A second key with the leads reversed does not plate, confirming that the object must be the cathode, and a plated and unplated key left in a damp place for a week compares rust resistance.
